steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a systematic literature review on human-centred learning analytics and AI in education. It should explain why the topic matters, what concerns motivate a human-centred approach, and what our review sets out to do.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- AI, learning analytics (LA) and AIED are transforming education
- Concerns raised by the spread of LA/AIED systems
- Human-centred design and Human-Centred AI (HCAI) as a response
- HCAI in LA/AIED: what the field has been doing
- Why a systematic literature review is needed now
- What this SLR does and contributes

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
AI is advancing fast and it is changing the way we do our daily activities. In education, AI and learning analytics (LA) innovations are bringing a big transformation, because they enable innovative teaching and learning strategies but at the same time they challenge current assessment practices. New LA and AI in Education (AIED) systems offer data-intensive solutions that promise adaptive and personalised teaching and learning experiences at scale. For example, there are various intelligent tutoring systems and LA solutions that give personalised learning support and automated feedback. LA dashboards give educators new ways to track student progress and give targeted support, which could lead to better student outcomes. LA and AIED systems combined with new interaction innovations like gamification and mixed reality also enable new pedagogical strategies that could make learning more engaging and interactive for students. So educational providers are adopting LA/AIED systems more and more, because data-intensive technologies promise to make learning more accessible, scalable, effective and personalised for students, and they do this through different teacher-facing and student-facing user interfaces.

But as LA/AIED systems spread there are key concerns about the privacy of students and the security of educational data, and also about algorithms possibly perpetuating biases and discrimination. Students and teachers are often not involved in the design and development of LA/AIED systems, and this can lead to them not understanding or not trusting the technology. This lack of involvement also raises questions about the accountability and transparency of AI in education. Also, students are adopting generative AI systems more, which may keep challenging existing assessment practices and blur the lines of academic integrity. So it is essential to address these concerns and to include the perspectives and authentic needs of students and teachers when LA/AIED systems are designed and implemented. This could help to create ethical, effective and inclusive ways to adopt LA/AIED systems.

Because of these challenges, there is a growing interest in human-centred design (HCD) approaches, which prioritise human needs, values and perspectives when LA/AIED systems are designed and deployed. Outside of education there is also growing interest in applying similar human-centred principles, in the emerging discipline of Human-Centred AI (HCAI). HCAI sees AI as systems that should serve human interests, and not as a way to reach technical goals or to replace humans. So the design of HCAI systems should be guided by ethical principles and design guidelines that empower end-users. The aim is to make sure that technologies with high automation capabilities are made in a way that guarantees that they are trustworthy, transparent and beneficial to society.

- HCAI in LA and AIED
  - growing recognition of stakeholders' needs and perspectives
  - participatory design / co-design with teachers, students, other stakeholders (educational decision-makers, learning designers, IT developers, educational researchers)
  - ethical frameworks tailored to LA and AIED
  - teachers' perspectives in ML algorithms and end-user LA interface designs
  - opening the algorithmic "black box" for teachers and students
- Need for an SLR
  - synthesise and evaluate existing research; guide future work, build on foundations
  - closest work: initial, non-systematic review of participatory and co-design of LA (design systems and techniques)
  - no comprehensive, systematic review of human-centred design / HCAI in LA/AIED
- This SLR
  - addresses knowledge gap on state of the art of human-centredness in LA/AIED
  - human-centred AI framework as lens
  - themes: human-centred design, human control vs computer automation, SRT; stakeholder involvement
  - findings: gaps, further investigation, methodological challenges; relevance and mainstream practice

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
AI is advancing fast and it is changing the way we do our daily activities. In education, AI and learning analytics (LA) innovations are bringing a big transformation, because they enable innovative teaching and learning strategies but at the same time they challenge current assessment practices. New LA and AI in Education (AIED) systems offer data-intensive solutions that promise adaptive and personalised teaching and learning experiences at scale. For example, there are various intelligent tutoring systems and LA solutions that give personalised learning support and automated feedback. LA dashboards give educators new ways to track student progress and give targeted support, which could lead to better student outcomes. LA and AIED systems combined with new interaction innovations like gamification and mixed reality also enable new pedagogical strategies that could make learning more engaging and interactive for students. So educational providers are adopting LA/AIED systems more and more, because data-intensive technologies promise to make learning more accessible, scalable, effective and personalised for students, and they do this through different teacher-facing and student-facing user interfaces.

But as LA/AIED systems spread there are key concerns about the privacy of students and the security of educational data, and also about algorithms possibly perpetuating biases and discrimination. Students and teachers are often not involved in the design and development of LA/AIED systems, and this can lead to them not understanding or not trusting the technology. This lack of involvement also raises questions about the accountability and transparency of AI in education. Also, students are adopting generative AI systems more, which may keep challenging existing assessment practices and blur the lines of academic integrity. So it is essential to address these concerns and to include the perspectives and authentic needs of students and teachers when LA/AIED systems are designed and implemented. This could help to create ethical, effective and inclusive ways to adopt LA/AIED systems.

Because of these challenges, there is a growing interest in human-centred design (HCD) approaches, which prioritise human needs, values and perspectives when LA/AIED systems are designed and deployed. Outside of education there is also growing interest in applying similar human-centred principles, in the emerging discipline of Human-Centred AI (HCAI). HCAI sees AI as systems that should serve human interests, and not as a way to reach technical goals or to replace humans. So the design of HCAI systems should be guided by ethical principles and design guidelines that empower end-users. The aim is to make sure that technologies with high automation capabilities are made in a way that guarantees that they are trustworthy, transparent and beneficial to society.

In recent years HCAI has got a lot of attention in LA and AIED, and there is more recognition that it is important to consider the needs and perspectives of educational stakeholders when data-intensive innovations are designed and deployed. One example is the use of participatory design and co-design methods to involve teachers, students and other educational stakeholders (such as educational decision-makers, learning designers, IT developers and educational researchers) in the co-creation of LA/AIED systems. There is also the development of ethical frameworks tailored to LA and AIED, work exploring new methods to bring teachers' perspectives and experiences into machine learning algorithms and end-user LA interface designs, and work on ways to open the AI algorithmic "black box" so teachers and students get insight into the analytics, or so the analysis outputs are communicated to them in ways that are easy to understand.

Since interest in applying human-centred design principles in LA/AIED research and practice is growing so fast, a systematic literature review (SLR) in this area is timely and gives an important opportunity to synthesise and evaluate the existing research. This can inform where future research goes and make sure new work builds on the foundations from previous studies. The closest work to ours is an earlier review, which did an initial, non-systematic review of the literature in participatory and co-design of LA. It surveyed the design systems and techniques used in the participatory design of learning analytics. As far as we know, no previous research has done a comprehensive and systematic review of the work that applies human-centred design and HCAI principles in the LA/AIED literature.

In this paper we present a SLR that goes beyond previous works and tries to address the knowledge gap about the state of the art of human-centredness in LA/AIED systems. We used the human-centred AI framework as a lens to motivate and structure our SLR. The framework helped us to focus on key themes of human-centred design, balancing human control and computer automation, and safety, reliability and trustworthiness (SRT), and to find relevant studies that address these themes in the context of stakeholder involvement in LA and AIED. The findings of this SLR give insights into gaps in the existing research, showing where more investigation is needed and which methodological challenges need to be addressed so that human-centred LA and AI in education data-intensive systems stay relevant and possibly become part of mainstream practice in the foreseeable future.

steps.text:
AI is advancing fast and it is changing the way we do our daily activities [1]. In education, AI and learning analytics (LA) innovations are bringing a big transformation, because they enable innovative teaching and learning strategies [2] but at the same time they challenge current assessment practices [3]. New LA and AI in Education (AIED) systems offer data-intensive solutions that promise adaptive and personalised teaching and learning experiences at scale. For example, there are various intelligent tutoring systems and LA solutions that give personalised learning support and automated feedback [4,5]. LA dashboards give educators new ways to track student progress and give targeted support, which could lead to better student outcomes [6,7]. LA and AIED systems combined with new interaction innovations like gamification and mixed reality [8] also enable new pedagogical strategies that could make learning more engaging and interactive for students. So educational providers are adopting LA/AIED systems more and more, because data-intensive technologies promise to make learning more accessible, scalable, effective and personalised for students [9], and they do this through different teacher-facing and student-facing user interfaces [10,11].

But as LA/AIED systems spread there are key concerns about the privacy of students and the security of educational data [12], and also about algorithms possibly perpetuating biases and discrimination [13]. So it is essential to address these concerns and to include the perspectives and authentic needs of students and teachers when LA/AIED systems are designed and implemented. This could help to create ethical, effective and inclusive ways to adopt LA/AIED systems [20,6].

Because of these challenges, there is a growing interest in human-centred design (HCD) approaches, which prioritise human needs, values and perspectives when LA/AIED systems are designed and deployed [21,22,23,24]. Outside of education there is also growing interest in applying similar human-centred principles, in the emerging discipline of Human-Centred AI (HCAI). HCAI sees AI as systems that should serve human interests, and not as a way to reach technical goals or to replace humans [25,26]. So the design of HCAI systems should be guided by ethical principles and design guidelines that empower end-users. The aim is to make sure that technologies with high automation capabilities are made in a way that guarantees that they are trustworthy, transparent and beneficial to society [26,27,28].

In recent years HCAI has got a lot of attention in LA and AIED, and there is more recognition that it is important to consider the needs and perspectives of educational stakeholders when data-intensive innovations are designed and deployed [24,29,16,30,31,32]. Since interest in applying human-centred design principles in LA/AIED research and practice is growing so fast, a systematic literature review (SLR) in this area is timely and gives an important opportunity to synthesise and evaluate the existing research. This can inform where future research goes and make sure new work builds on the foundations from previous studies. The closest work to ours is [16], which did an initial, non-systematic review of the literature in participatory and co-design of LA. It surveyed the design systems and techniques used in the participatory design of learning analytics. As far as we know, no previous research has done a comprehensive and systematic review of the work that applies human-centred design and HCAI principles in the LA/AIED literature.

In this paper we present a SLR that goes beyond previous works and tries to address the knowledge gap about the state of the art of human-centredness in LA/AIED systems. We used the human-centred AI framework [25] as a lens to motivate and structure our SLR. The framework helped us to focus on key themes of human-centred design, balancing human control and computer automation, and safety, reliability and trustworthiness (SRT), and to find relevant studies that address these themes in the context of stakeholder involvement in LA and AIED. The findings of this SLR give insights into gaps in the existing research, showing where more investigation is needed and which methodological challenges need to be addressed so that human-centred LA and AI in education data-intensive systems stay relevant and possibly become part of mainstream practice in the foreseeable future.

steps.text:
Advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) are rapidly changing how we carry out our daily activities [1]. In educational contexts, AI and learning analytics (LA) innovations are prompting a significant transformation, both enabling innovative teaching and learning strategies [2] and at the same time challenging current assessment practices [3]. Emerging LA and AI in Education (AIED) systems offer novel data-intensive solutions that promise to enable adaptive and personalised teaching and learning experiences at scale. For instance, various intelligent tutoring systems and LA solutions provide personalised learning support and automated feedback [4,5]. LA dashboards give educators new means to track student progress and offer targeted support, potentially leading to improved student outcomes [6,7]. LA and AIED systems, paired with novel interaction innovations such as gamification and mixed reality [8], are also enabling new pedagogical strategies that can potentially make learning more engaging and interactive for students. In sum, educational providers are increasingly adopting LA/AIED systems because data-intensive technologies promise to make learning more accessible, scalable, effective, and personalised for students [9] through various forms of teacher-facing and student-facing user interfaces [10,11].

Yet the proliferation of LA/AIED systems raises key concerns about the privacy of students and the security of educational data [12], as well as the potential for algorithms to perpetuate biases and discrimination [13]. The lack of involvement of students and teachers in the design and development of LA/AIED systems can lead to a lack of understanding and trust in the technology [14,15,16,17]. This lack of involvement also raises questions about the accountability and transparency of AI in education [18]. Furthermore, increased student adoption of generative AI systems may recurrently challenge existing assessment practices and blur the lines of academic integrity [19]. It is thus essential to address these concerns and to incorporate the perspectives and authentic needs of students and teachers when designing and implementing LA/AIED systems. This can contribute to creating ethical, effective, and inclusive ways to adopt LA/AIED systems [20,6].

In response to these challenges, there has been a growing interest in adopting human-centred design (HCD) approaches that prioritise human needs, values, and perspectives in the design and deployment of LA/AIED systems [21,22,23,24]. Beyond education, there is also a growing interest in applying similar human-centred principles in the emerging discipline of Human-Centred AI (HCAI). An HCAI approach views AI as systems aimed at serving human interests rather than as a means of achieving technical goals or replacing humans [25,26]. The design of HCAI systems is therefore to be guided by a set of ethical principles and design guidelines that empower end-users, with the aim of ensuring that technologies with high automation capabilities are created in ways that guarantee their trustworthiness, transparency, and benefit to society [26,27,28].

In recent years, HCAI has gained significant attention in LA and AIED, with a growing recognition of the importance of considering educational stakeholders’ needs and perspectives in the design and deployment of data-intensive innovations [24,29,16,30,31,32]. This includes, for example, the use of participatory design and co-design methods to involve teachers [33,34], students [35,36], and other educational stakeholders (such as educational decision-makers, learning designers, IT developers and educational researchers) [37,38] in the co-creation of LA/AIED systems; the development of ethical frameworks tailored to LA and AIED [15,30,39]; the exploration of new methods for incorporating teachers' perspectives and experiences into machine learning algorithms and end-user LA interface designs [23,40]; and ways to open the AI algorithmic "black box" to give teachers and students insight into the analytics or to communicate analysis outputs to them in ways they can easily understand [41].

Given the rapidly growing interest in applying human-centred design principles in LA/AIED research and practice, a timely systematic literature review (SLR) in this area offers an important opportunity to synthesise and evaluate the existing body of research. This can inform the direction of future research and ensure that new work builds upon the foundations established by previous studies. The closest work to ours was presented by [16], who conducted an initial, non-systematic review of the literature in participatory and co-design of LA, surveying the design systems and techniques used in the participatory design of learning analytics. To the best of our knowledge, no previous research has conducted a comprehensive and systematic review of the body of work applying human-centred design and HCAI principles in the LA/AIED literature.

This paper presents a SLR that goes beyond previous works and aims to address the knowledge gap about the state of the art of human-centredness in LA/AIED systems. We used the human-centred AI framework [25] as a lens to motivate and structure our SLR. This framework helped us focus on the key themes of human-centred design, balancing human control and computer automation, and safety, reliability, and trustworthiness (SRT), and to identify relevant studies addressing these themes in the context of stakeholder involvement in LA and AIED. The findings of this SLR contribute insights into gaps in the existing research, highlighting areas where further investigation is needed and methodological challenges that must be addressed for human-centred LA and AI in education data-intensive systems to remain relevant and potentially become part of mainstream practice in the foreseeable future.
